items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.link_text: 1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County

entry.rationale: Tree fact F2 records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, cited to S3 (PA Death Certificates). Statewide registration began 1906 (loc_001), so this certificate exists; re-read the image for the parents and birthplace fields and the informant, since the tree records the death but not who is named as parent. The collection 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968' is name-searchable. Note the tree's birth place (Ireland, F1) differs from the objective's 'PA'; the certificate's birthplace helps settle this.

Requested by the researcher. Ancestry's '1870 United States Federal Census' (paid, index) should show Patrick (about 25) either in a parental household or his own, with birthplace and neighbors. 1870 does not state relationships, so a household with Thomas Flynn is consistent with, not proof of, parentage. Tree already holds 1850 and 1860 census as sources for the Thomas-Patrick link (S1, S2); 1850 and 1860 name no relationships, so that link is not yet documented by a record stating it. Try Flynn variants (Flinn, Flin, Fleming, Flyn).

The 1880 census is the first to record relationship to head and parents' birthplaces, so Patrick, or a parent living with him, would be stated directly. Fills the later part of the window, between the 1870 census and the 1908 death. Search by name with variants; verify against the image.

Irish-born family likely Roman Catholic; per loc_001 registers sit with parishes of the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county. The name-searchable Schuylkill County Church Records collection may hold Patrick's marriage, children's baptisms (sponsors, parents' names), his burial in 1908, and siblings' or Thomas's entries. Pre-1906 events rely on church records. If the birth was in Ireland, a Pennsylvania baptism will not exist, so the burial and marriage entries are the route to origin.

Patrick's own marriage (about age 20-40): marriage entries often state age, birthplace and parents' names. Search 'Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950' and 'Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900' (name-searchable; compiled is leads only). County Marriages 1885-1950 only covers later marriages. Tree has no spouse for Patrick, so spouse identity is also unknown.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (tree: born about 1818, Ireland) to Patrick's mother, a woman whose name is not in the tree. It would confirm them as a couple, supply her name (maiden name only if this was her first marriage; search also for any other marriage of hers), and its date relative to about 1845 would corroborate the link. It does not alone prove Patrick is their child. Marriage may have occurred in Ireland, so a church-record search in Pennsylvania is paired with Civil and Compiled Marriages. Thomas as Patrick's father is not yet documented by a parentage-stating record.

Register of Wills records from 1811 (loc_001) can name heirs. Window set by Thomas's lifespan (born about 1818, so death could fall to roughly 1900 or beyond), not Patrick's. 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' is browse-only (personCount 0), so an image browse of the county volumes. Also check for Patrick's own estate (1908).

FAN and survivors item: an obituary or death notice for Patrick (March 1908) or for Thomas would name surviving siblings, spouse and children, whose own records (baptism, marriage, death certificates) can name the same parents. Also check cemetery or burial records for plot-mates and family members. Siblings' records bear directly on the subject's parentage.

---

## What the tree already holds

- **Patrick Flynn (I2):** Birth ~1845 in Ireland (note: the question text says PA, which conflicts with the tree). Death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, from a PA death certificate.

---

| # | Item | Type | Repository |
|---|------|------|------------|
| 1 | **pli_004** | Vital record — 1908 PA death certificate | FamilySearch |
| 2 | **pli_005** | Church — burial/cemetery, Schuylkill County | FamilySearch |
| 3 | **pli_006** | Vital record — Patrick's marriage(s), 1865–1908 | FamilySearch |
| 4 | **pli_007** | Census — 1860, 1870, 1880 households | FamilySearch |
| 5 | **pli_008** | Vital record — Thomas Flynn's marriage (Patrick's parents' marriage, 1835–1850) | FamilySearch |

collections.title: Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Mode: create. Question: q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?" The plan is pl_002.

**What the tree already holds**
- Patrick (I1): birth ~1845 in Ireland (F1, from the 1850 census). Death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (F2, from the PA death certificate, S3). The question text says he was born in Pennsylvania, which conflicts with the tree.
- Thomas Flynn (I2): born ~1818 in Ireland. The tree links him as Patrick's father (R1), but that link rests on household position in the 1850 census (a_004), which names no relationships.
- 1850 census: Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84, family 91. 1860 census: attached as S2 but never searched, so the 1851-1860 timeline gap is open.
- Log: three searches, all of the 1850 census (FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage). No other record type has been searched.
- The subject has no FamilySearch ark, so there is no hints item. The subject is a project subject, so I did not read his FamilySearch profile.
- The US military wiki page was not found. It was not required, because Patrick was born in Ireland and is a British Isles case.

**Plan pl_002, in order**
1. pli_004, vital_record, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. The 1908 death certificate (name-searchable) should give parents' names and the informant.
2. pli_005, church, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Patrick's own burial entry, plus cemetery records. A Pennsylvania baptism may not exist for an Irish-born man, so this works back from the end of his life.
3. pli_006, vital_record, FamilySearch. Patrick's own marriage(s), 1865-1908, which may state his birthplace or parents.
4. pli_007, census, FamilySearch. 1860, 1870 and 1880 households. The 1880 census records relationship to the head.
5. pli_008, vital_record, FamilySearch. The marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother (the dedicated parents' marriage item), 1835-1850. It confirms the couple but does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. No surname found is to be called her maiden name without an earlier-marriage check. A marriage in Ireland would need a locality survey first.
6. pli_009, probate, FamilySearch. Wills or administrations for Thomas and for Patrick, 1850-1908. This collection is browse-only (personCount 0), so it is an image browse.
7. pli_010, court (naturalization), FamilySearch. This is the FAN item, along with neighbors and siblings. Naturalization records are browse-only image groups.

No item is a fallback. There are nine searches, and the plan covers more than census and vital records.

The Irish-origin records need a locality survey for Ireland before they can be planned.

Hand-back: search-records for items 1 to 8 (FamilySearch), and search-external-sites for pli_012.

---

It then looks at his marriage and the later censuses. After that come the marriage of Thomas to Patrick's mother, wills and estates, immigration and naturalization papers, church texts searched for the family names, and a newspaper obituary.

Next, I would start with the 1908 death certificate and burial entry.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.link_text: Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801
1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County

entry.rationale: Tree fact F2 records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, cited to S3 (PA death certificates). Statewide registration began 1906 (loc_001), so a 1908 state certificate exists; the collection 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968' is name-searchable. Read the image for informant, birthplace and parents' names; the informant is also a FAN lead. Verify the tree's existing parent link against the image rather than assume it.

Patrick's own burial entry. The tree gives his birth as ~1845 in Ireland (F1, from the 1850 census), so a Pennsylvania baptism probably does not exist and an Irish register is unknown; burial and death entries often state age or birthplace. The Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable. Catholic registers sit with the Diocese/Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county (loc_001), so also check parish holdings. Note the question text says born in PA while the tree says Ireland: a premise to test.

The tree cites 1850 and 1860 census (S1, S2) and q_002 covers 1850; here, the 1870 and 1880 enumerations. 1880 records relationship to head and each person's parents' birthplaces, and shows whether Thomas Flynn and a wife remained in the household. Thomas is in the tree only as a parent with birth ~1818 Ireland, supported by census sources alone. The 1870 is also available on Ancestry (paid index). Use name variants Flinn, Flin, Flynn, Fflynn, Patt/Patrick.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (Thomas Flynn and a wife not yet named). It would confirm them as a couple, supply the wife's surname (only if this was her first marriage, which is untested, so do not call any surname a maiden name), and by date relative to ~1845 corroborate the link. It does not alone show Patrick is their child. Given an Irish birth ~1845 the marriage may be in Ireland, outside PA records; search Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (name-searchable) and Catholic church registers, and look for any earlier marriage of the wife.

Register of Wills holds probate from 1811 (loc_001). 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse the Schuylkill dockets and indexes image by image. Window is set by Thomas Flynn's lifespan (born ~1818, death plausible up to ~1900) plus Patrick's own estate to 1908; a will or administration naming heirs is direct parentage evidence. Also covers the wife's estate.

Patrick's own marriage record(s), church or civil (County Marriages 1885-1950 is name-searchable; earlier marriages in church registers). Marriage entries may name parents or a home parish, a usual route to origin when no baptism exists. Also reveals the spouse's family as FAN and any earlier marriage.

FAN item: siblings' baptisms and marriages, and burials of other Flynns in the household found in the censuses, naming the same parents; also sponsors/godparents and neighbours in the Irish coal-region parish. Sibling records can place a child with parents, which the parents' marriage cannot. Use Flynn/Flinn variants.

Naturalization of Thomas Flynn and of Patrick (if foreign-born per F1) in the county courts and passenger arrivals at Philadelphia or New York; may state origin parish or county in Ireland. loc_001 flags coal-region naturalization films as browse-only image groups, so check volume_search for the county and browse. Window runs to Patrick's later life, as naturalization could be decades after arrival.

  - Statewide death registration began in 1906.

**Plan pl_002 (items in order)**
- **pli_004**, vital_record, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch: the 1908 death certificate. It may name the informant, birthplace and parents.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.informant: Unknown informant (most likely a household member, possibly a neighbor) reporting to census enumerator
items.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. The person who provided the name is unknown — most likely a household member, possibly a neighbor. Proximity is 'unknown' rather than 'household_member' because for names specifically, the enumerator may have heard the name from a neighbor or made an assumption — the name fact doesn't necessarily require active reporting the way age/birthplace does.

items.informant: Unknown — most likely a household member (such as Thomas Flynn or his wife), but possibly a neighbor
items.informant_bias_notes: Age and birthplace require active reporting by an informant — someone had to tell the enumerator these facts. That informant was most likely a household member, but enumerators also took information from neighbors when residents were unavailable, and the census does not identify who answered. Proximity is 'unknown' because the informant cannot be established from the record.

items.informant: Census enumerator (witness to residence by visiting the dwelling)

- He died on 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County. The certificate names Thomas Flynn as his father and gives no mother.
- Thomas Flynn (I2) was born about 1818 in Ireland. The tree links him as Patrick's father only from census household position (a relationship the census does not state) and from that secondary certificate statement.
- The 1850 and 1860 censuses are done, so the plan has no census items. The 1860–1908 gap in the timeline is high severity. The plan fills it through church, probate and marriage records.
- I1 has no FamilySearch ark, so I added no hints-review item.

- **pli_006:** church, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Patrick's own marriage and his children's baptisms, in a name-searchable collection, with Flynn spelling variants.
- **pli_007:** church, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Patrick's own burial entry, dated 1908. His baptism probably does not exist in reach, because he was born in Ireland and no Irish parish is known.
- **pli_008:** church, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. The marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife to each other. It would confirm the couple and name the mother, but alone it does not prove Patrick is their child.
- **pli_009:** probate, Schuylkill Register of Wills, FamilySearch. Thomas Flynn's will or administration. The collection is browse-only (personCount 0). The date range is sized to Thomas's lifespan, 1860–1910.
- **pli_010:** probate, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Patrick's own 1908 estate, browse-only (personCount 0), for heirs and surviving siblings.
- **pli_011:** church, FamilySearch. FAN search on possible siblings from the 1850 and 1860 households and on Patrick's daughter's marriage to James Brown. These entries often name both parents.
- **pli_012:** church, via the full-text search skill. Unscoped co-occurrence search on Patrick and Thomas Flynn plus Ireland, to find their county or parish of origin.
- **pli_013:** immigration, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Naturalization records for Thomas and/or Patrick. These are browse-only image groups per the locality guide.
- **pli_014:** newspaper, other repository. Patrick's 1908 obituary. This is lower priority because access is uncertain.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Mode: add-new. The earlier plan (pl_002) for q_001 had all items completed, so I wrote a new active plan, pl_003, built around the FAN approach. Question q_001: "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

- Thomas Flynn is recorded as his father, born about 1818 in Ireland. The link rests on the 1850 census, the 1860 census and the 1908 death certificate.
- The 1850 census puts Patrick, age 5, in Thomas's household (dwelling 84). The 1860 census puts him there at age 15 (dwelling 112). Neither census states relationships.
- The 1908 death certificate names Thomas as father. The informant was Patrick's son-in-law, James Brown, so the information is secondhand. The certificate gives Pennsylvania as Patrick's birthplace, which conflicts with the censuses (Ireland).
- The proof summary rates the conclusion "probable". The 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses and Thomas's probate have not been searched. The timeline shows a high-severity gap from 1860 to 1908.
- Patrick's mother is unnamed in every record so far.
- Patrick has no FamilySearch ark, so I added no hints-review item.
- Because he was probably born in Ireland, a Pennsylvania baptism may not exist. I therefore planned his own burial entry (pli_008).

**Plan pl_003, in execution order**
1. pli_006: census, Schuylkill County, 1850–1860, FamilySearch. Re-open the two schedules and transcribe the neighbouring households and any other adults in the Flynn dwelling.
2. pli_007: church, Schuylkill County, 1845–1908, FamilySearch. Look for Flynn siblings' baptisms and sponsors. The Church Records collection is name-searchable.
3. pli_008: church and cemetery, 1908, FamilySearch. This is Patrick's own burial entry, for age, birthplace and who arranged the burial.
4. pli_015: vital_record, 1835–1850, FamilySearch. This is the dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother. It allows for an Irish marriage or an earlier or later marriage of the mother. A marriage alone does not prove Patrick is their child.
5. pli_009: vital_record, 1865–1900, FamilySearch. Patrick's own marriage, with its witnesses and his wife's family.
6. pli_010: vital_record, 1880–1930, FamilySearch. James Brown's marriage, plus death certificates of Patrick's children and any Flynn siblings. These may name his mother.
7. pli_011: probate, 1850–1908, FamilySearch. Browse Thomas's will or administration, sized to Thomas's lifespan. The probate collection is `browse-only (personCount 0)`. It names heirs, witnesses and appraisers.
8. pli_012: census, 1870–1900, FamilySearch. The 1880 census records relationships, so it may show Patrick as "son".
9. pli_013: immigration (naturalization), 1840–1900, FamilySearch. Naturalizations of Thomas and Patrick and their witnesses. This is browse-only, so pair it with an image browse.
10. pli_014: newspaper, 1908, other repository. Patrick's obituary, for surviving relatives and pallbearers.

Two things to note. I could not find a way to put pli_015 in sequence position 4, so it carries sequence 5 like pli_009 and the order is approximate. I did not call `person_read`, because Patrick is a project subject. I also did not fetch the wiki pages: the subject is a male born in Ireland, and neither the military nor the naming-customs trigger applies.

Hand-back: search-records for the FamilySearch items, and search-external-sites for the newspaper item.

# Locality Guide: Feliciana Parish / East and West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana (1810-1835)

Feliciana Parish split into East and West Feliciana Parish in 1824. This is a geographic split: which successor parish holds a given record depends on where within the old parish the event occurred, and that is frequently unknown. Records for a family resident in the old parish before 1824 may be found under either successor's name after that date — search both.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

sources.title: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Deed Records, 1875, Patrick Sheahan purchase
sources.citation: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, Recorder of Deeds, Deed Book 42, p. 118, Patrick Sheahan from James Kelly, 1875; FamilySearch digital images.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree fact F1 records Michael resident in Pennsylvania in 1870 and F2/F3 record him in Schuylkill County in 1882 as a miner; log_001 shows a farmer outside Schuylkill in 1870. United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable. Finding him (or not) in Schuylkill in 1880 tests whether the move really fell near 1882 and, if he is elsewhere, names the last pre-move residence, occupation and household. Search Sheahan/Shehan/Sheehan/Shean variants. loc_001 gives Schuylkill as formed 1811, so no boundary split affects 1880.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. Catholic registers (loc_001: Philadelphia archdiocese, held at parish) may show Michael as sponsor, parent or burial, naming his prior parish or origin, and may show ties to Patrick. Variant spellings required. Pair with browse of the church image group (record-searchable 0%, 1842-1895) if the name search underdelivers.

FAN item. Tree fact F4 (source S1) records brother Patrick Sheahan buying land from James Kelly in Schuylkill in 1875, Deed Book 42 p. 118. Michael may have followed his brother; read that deed for witnesses, neighbors and residence of the grantor/grantee, and browse the deed image group (partly record-searchable, 22%) for Michael or Patrick transactions or leases through 1900. loc_001 notes laborers often leased from mining companies, so a missing deed for Michael does not contradict mining work.

Michael's own marriage entry: if he married near the move (the Schuylkill marriage image group covers 1870-1910, record-searchable 0%; Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 and Civil Marriages 1677-1950 are name-searchable), it may state residence, occupation, birthplace, parents and witnesses (FAN, possibly Patrick). A bride from the coal region would suggest a different motive than work alone.

Michael's own death or burial entry. Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906-1968 is name-searchable and gives birthplace, years of residence, parents and occupation; for deaths before 1906 (statewide registration began 1906 per loc_001) use church burial entries and cemetery records. Window begins after the 1882 last-known date and runs to a plausible old age.

United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable and records occupation, years married, birthplace and, if foreign-born, year of immigration, plus neighbors who may be Patrick or other kin. Shows whether mining work persisted after the move. Covers the later part of the question window.

Naturalization image group (browse-only, record-searchable 0%, loc_001 notes these are browse image-by-image). If Michael was foreign-born, a declaration or petition gives birthplace, arrival date and prior residence, and witnesses (FAN). Skip with reason if the 1880 or 1900 census show him native-born.

Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), as is the Schuylkill probate image group. Estate files of Patrick, Michael or their parent (unnamed, tree person I3) may name heirs, residences and mining-related debts or employers. Window sized to the creators' lifespans (a parent could die up to 60 years after the 1882 move), not the 1882 event.

Outside FamilySearch: Schuylkill local newspapers, coal-company employee or payroll records, mine inspector accident reports and county histories (Pennsylvania state archives or local historical society, to be located by the researcher). These could document hiring, strikes or mine openings around 1882 and any mention of Michael or Patrick, the only direct route to cause rather than just the fact of a move. Family tradition itself is a lead, not evidence.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

Also search Patrick Sheahan (Schuylkill resident 1875 per tree). Try Sheahan, Shehan, Sheehan, Shehon variants.

Deed Records 1815-1900 volume is mostly browse-only (about 22 percent record-searchable): search Michael/Patrick/James Kelly in grantor-grantee indexes, then browse. Per loc_001 laborers often leased rather than bought, so absence is not negative evidence. Look for Michael as grantee, witness or neighbor in boundary recitals.

entry.rationale: Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable; loc_001 says registers stay with the parish/diocese, not Scranton. Marriages, baptisms of children and sponsors, and burials of Michael, spouse or Patrick show parish, mining town and associates, and may name origin or relatives. Also a browse-only church volume (1842-1895, personCount 0 equivalent) for parishes not indexed.

Michael's own marriage (if after 1870): Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 and Civil Marriages are name-searchable; the 1870-1910 Schuylkill marriage volume is browse-only (personCount 0). Entries may give residence, occupation (miner), birthplace and parents, and witnesses who may be the Patrick/Kelly circle. Pre-1906 civil birth/death registration does not exist (loc_001).

United States Census, 1900 (name-searchable) records occupation, months unemployed, immigration year and years in the US for Michael and household; shows whether he stayed a miner and neighbors (fellow miners, relatives). Directly tests whether Michael worked at a named colliery and when. Free FamilySearch items first, paid newspaper sites after.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.question: Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?
items.rationale: log_001 places Michael as a farmer in a different county in 1870; log_002 places him in Schuylkill County by 1882 with occupation 'miner'. The occupation and location both changed between these two points, consistent with a work-driven relocation to the anthracite coal region, but nothing yet directly documents the move itself or its cause -- no land purchase, employment record, or correspondence has been found. No plan has yet been written for this question.

entry.rationale: Tree fact F1 records only a 1870 residence 'Pennsylvania' with no county; log_001 says farmer in a different county. United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable and would fix his county, household and occupation before the move, giving the anchor from which to test a work-driven relocation. Try variant spellings (Sheahan, Shehan, Sheehan, Shean).

Tree fact F2/F3 place him in Schuylkill County in 1882 as a miner. United States Census, 1880 (name-searchable) falls inside the gap: if he is still in the old county in June 1880, the move is post-1880; if in Schuylkill already, the 1882 date is wrong. Records relationship to head and occupation. Search statewide first since the county is the unknown.

United States Census, 1900 (name-searchable; the 1890 schedules are largely lost) shows whether he remained a miner after the move, plus birthplace, immigration year and naturalization status, and neighbors/boarders who may be co-workers or kin from the same origin (FAN). Window sized past 1882 because later records testify to the occupation.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. loc_001: Catholic registers stay with the Archdiocese of Philadelphia parishes, not the county. Baptisms of his children, his marriage, or burial entries name residences and parishes and may state a prior home; mining-patch parishes also show where he settled.

His own marriage and death entries. Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 and Civil Marriages 1677-1950 are name-searchable; Death Certificates 1906-1968 is name-searchable. loc_001: civil death registration began only in 1906, so earlier death falls to church/cemetery items. Death certificates often state birthplace, parents and occupation (e.g. coal miner); a miner's cause of death may note mine accident or miners' asthma.

Local anthracite-region newspapers (e.g. Pottsville papers, to be located via the FamilySearch catalog or Chronicling America/Newspapers.com) report mine accidents, strikes, hiring and obituaries naming employer and mine. An obituary or accident notice could directly state his occupation and arrival; newspaper availability must be confirmed.

Employment evidence: Pennsylvania Inspector of Mines annual reports (list collieries, fatalities and injuries by name), colliery/coal company payroll and employment ledgers (e.g. Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Co. records, held at repositories such as Hagley or the Schuylkill County Historical Society, to be located). This is the only record type that directly documents mine work and employer in 1882.

Naturalization (if foreign-born, as the Sheahan name suggests but is unproven) and county court records. loc_001: coal-region naturalization films are browse-only image groups, so plan an image-by-image browse via volume_search, not a name search. Declarations state arrival date, prior residence and sometimes witnesses (fellow miners, FAN).

Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0): browse Schuylkill wills/estates up to his plausible death. Inventories show occupation, leased versus owned land (loc_001: laborers mostly leased from mining companies, so deeds are unlikely) and heirs who may be the family-tradition source.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree records Patrick Flynn b. ~1845 Ireland (S1, 1850 census) and Thomas Flynn b. ~1818 Ireland as father (R1, cited to 1850, 1860 census and death certificate). The 1860 census and 1908 death certificate are already searched (pli_004, pli_005). United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable; it names every household member with age and birthplace but not relationships, so a Thomas of about 52 born in Ireland in Patrick's household or next door is consistent with, not proof of, parentage. Search Patrick Flynn, Flynn/Flinn/Flin/Flyn variants, b. 1843-1847, Irish-born, starting in Schuylkill and widening to adjacent coal-region counties since the loc_001 anthracite-region setting makes mobility likely. Patrick would be about 25 and may be married with his own household.

United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable and is the first schedule to record relationship to head, so a Thomas Flynn (about 62, Irish-born) listed as father or father-in-law in Patrick's household would be direct evidence of the relationship; it also records parents' birthplaces. Same variant spellings; follow the household found in 1870, or search anew if not found.

United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable, records relationship to head, birth month and year, years married and immigration year. It is the last census before Patrick's 1908 death, so it fixes his household and his own birth year/immigration year (useful for finding the Irish origin). Note the 1890 census was destroyed, so there is no census between 1880 and 1900; the gap is covered by items below. Thomas would be about 82 if alive.

Per loc_001, the county Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811 and these name heirs. Window is set by Thomas Flynn's plausible death (b. ~1818, alive in 1860 per tree, so death 1860 to about 1905) and by Patrick's 1908 death. Search both men; a will or administration naming Patrick as son would be direct parentage evidence, and the 1870/1880/1900 results narrow the likely death window for Thomas.

Patrick's birth is recorded as Ireland, so a Pennsylvania baptism may not exist; the 1908 death certificate is already searched. Look for his own burial entry (1908) and marriage entry in the Catholic parish registers, which loc_001 notes are held by the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county. They often give age and Irish origin, and a burial/cemetery entry may place Thomas in the same plot. Also check Thomas Flynn's burial entry from 1860 onward.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother (est. 1835-1845, in Ireland or an early Pennsylvania parish). It would confirm the couple as a unit, give the mother's maiden name (no 1850-1900 census gives it), and date the union against Patrick's ~1845 birth. It does not alone prove Patrick is their child; the 1880 relationship column or a probate record is needed. Treat any surname given for the mother as possibly a prior married name.

FAN item: using households found in items 1-3, record the neighbors, boarders and in-laws for Patrick (same-surname Flynns, Irish neighbors, a wife's family). These people may be siblings or Thomas's relatives and will be the targets of sibling baptism/marriage records naming the same parents. Also use the same pass to check for a Thomas Flynn in a nearby household, since the 1870 and 1880 schedules were not necessarily taken with elders in the son's home.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree records Patrick's death 12 Mar 1908 in Schuylkill County (S3, PA Death Certificates). Per loc_001 statewide registration began 1906, so a certificate exists; it normally names father and mother (maiden name) and birthplace, but the informant's knowledge is secondary. Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable. Verify against the image; note the question says born PA while the tree says Ireland ~1845, a birthplace discrepancy to test.

Patrick's own burial/funeral entry, planned because a baptism may not exist: tree birth ~1845 is in Ireland (S1), outside any PA register. loc_001: Catholic registers are held at the parish/archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county. Burial entries may state age, native parish or parents. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable; also check cemetery records.

Patrick's own marriage (church or civil), planned because a baptism may not exist. Marriage entries often state age, birthplace and parents' names. Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 and Civil Marriages 1677-1950 are name-searchable; earlier Catholic marriages are in the church register collection. Try variants Flynn/Flinn/Flin/O'Flynn.

Tree cites the 1850 and 1860 census (S1, S2) for the Patrick-Thomas link, but the 1850 census names only the head with relationship unstated, so that is not yet proof of parentage. 1880 census gives relationship to head and parents' birthplaces; 1860/1870 show household composition (siblings, mother's given name). External collection also available for census at Ancestry/MyHeritage as alternate indexes.

Dedicated item: marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland, tree) to Patrick's mother. It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's name (only if her first marriage; watch for remarriage, so do not assume the surname is her birth name), and its date relative to ~1845 corroborates parentage, though it does not by itself show Patrick is their child. May fall in Ireland or PA; search PA Civil/Compiled Marriages and the Schuylkill church collection, all name-searchable.

Estate of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, tree) at the county Register of Wills (held from 1811 per loc_001); window set by Thomas's plausible lifespan to ~1905, not Patrick's. A will or administration naming Patrick as heir would be direct evidence. Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0): browse the Schuylkill dockets and indexes image by image. Also check mother's estate.

FAN item: baptisms, marriages and burials of Patrick's possible siblings, and sponsors/witnesses, naming Thomas Flynn and a wife as parents. Records placing other children with the couple, plus sponsors who were kin, bear on whether Patrick belongs to this family. Name-searchable Schuylkill church collection; check Catholic parish registers via Archdiocese of Philadelphia per loc_001.

Naturalization of Patrick or Thomas Flynn: tree gives Irish birth, and declarations may name the origin county/parish and arrival date, the route to an Irish origin. loc_001 says coal-region naturalization films are browse-only (~0% record-searchable), so browse county court naturalization volumes image by image (use volume_search to locate them).

Full-text co-occurrence search (run via search-full-text, unscoped across the corpus) on the surnames Flynn and the mother's name once found, with Patrick and Thomas as separate required terms, to catch church acts in the PA or Irish origin where name indexing fails. Fallback if indexed searches in items 1-7 do not name parents.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Bridget (b. ~1838 Ireland), John Doyle (no dates) and Ellen. log_003 shows Ellen's marriage record naming John Doyle and Bridget Halloran, so the Doyle household was likely intact in 1870. United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable. Search Doyle households with Bridget ~32 and John, in Schuylkill County, with variants Doyl/Doyel/Dolan and Halloran/Holloran; list every child in the household (1870 names all members; relationship not stated, so infer cautiously).

United States Census, 1860 is name-searchable and would catch the earliest children if John and Bridget married by the late 1850s. 1860 names every household member with age and birthplace; relationship is not stated. Search the same name variants; the household may sit in a coal-region township, so search the county broadly.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth registration began only in 1906 (loc_001), so baptisms are the primary birth evidence. Catholic registers stay at the parish under the Archdiocese of Philadelphia (loc_001). The collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' is name-searchable. Search baptisms with father John Doyle, mother Bridget Halloran/Holloran; sponsors are FAN leads. Registers can give the mother's maiden name, tying children to this couple.

Bridget married Martin Kearney in 1879 (log_001), so surviving Doyle children may appear in the 1880 Kearney household as stepchildren. 1880 is the first census recording relationship to head. United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable. Search Martin Kearney with wife Bridget in Schuylkill County, and also Doyle children living elsewhere in service or with relatives.

FAN and sibling item: marriages of Doyle children name John Doyle and Bridget Halloran as parents, as Ellen's did (log_003). Search Pennsylvania County Marriages for brides and grooms surnamed Doyle with those parents, plus Kearney stepchildren. Window runs to 1915 because 9 children bore from ~1855 to ~1878 and surviving ones married as late as 1900s. Only 2 of 9 lived to 1900 (log_002), so many may have died young; the marriages identify the survivors.

Burial entries for John Doyle (died before the 1879 remarriage, which log_001 implies) and for infant or child Doyles. Bridget reported 9 births with 2 living in 1900 (log_002), so ~7 children died, mostly leaving only burial entries naming parents. Name-searchable church collection; this is the route for children who died before any census.

Estate or administration of John Doyle (died before 1879) held by the county Register of Wills (loc_001), which would name the widow and all heirs. Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of Schuylkill County docket and administration volumes, not a name search.

Probate of Bridget (Halloran Doyle) Kearney and of Martin Kearney, window sized to Bridget's plausible lifespan (b. ~1838, living 1900) not the children's births. Wills or administrations name surviving children by both marriages. Browse-only (personCount 0) collection; image browse of Schuylkill docket indexes.

Cemetery and headstone records for John Doyle, Bridget Kearney and Doyle children, including infants, which are buried in the family plot; markers and sexton records can name children with no other record. Search Catholic cemeteries in Schuylkill County; plot neighbors are FAN leads.

Obituaries and death notices for John Doyle, Doyle children and Bridget Kearney in Schuylkill County papers (anthracite-region weeklies). Notices often list surviving children and siblings, and cover deaths before 1906 where no civil death record exists (loc_001).

agent_returns.text:
Mode: create. I wrote the plan but did not run any searches.

**Question q_001:** "Who were the other children born to Bridget Halloran and her first husband, John Doyle, beyond the one already identified (Ellen Doyle)?"

**Why I stopped short of searching:** executing searches belongs to search-records, and I can't run them from here. Please hand pl_001 to search-records for the FamilySearch items (pli_001 to pli_008). Items pli_009 and pli_010 are external-site items for search-external-sites. I did not ask you anything first, as you requested.

**What the project already records**
- Bridget Halloran was born about 1838 in Ireland. The project tree has no dates for John Doyle or Ellen.
- log_001: Bridget, shown as "Bridget (Doyle) Halloran", married Martin Kearney in Schuylkill County in 1879. That makes John Doyle's death or departure fall before 1879.
- log_002: the 1900 census shows Bridget as mother of 9 children, 2 living. That leaves about 7 children unidentified, probably dead young.
- log_003: Ellen Doyle's marriage record (1865–1875 search window) names her parents as John Doyle and Bridget Halloran.
- The tree has no attached sources.
- The Pennsylvania probate collection is browse-only (personCount 0). The Schuylkill church collection and the 1860, 1870, 1880 and 1900 census collections are name-searchable.

**Plan pl_001, in execution order**
- pli_001: census, Schuylkill, FamilySearch, 1870. Find the Doyle household and list every child.
- pli_002: census, Schuylkill, FamilySearch, 1860. Catches the earliest children.
- pli_003: church baptisms, Schuylkill, FamilySearch, 1855–1880. Statewide civil birth registration only began in 1906, so baptisms are the birth evidence. Parents' names tie each child to this couple.
- pli_004: census, Schuylkill, FamilySearch, 1880. Surviving Doyle children may be stepchildren in the Kearney household, and 1880 records relationship to the head.
- pli_005: marriages of Doyle children, FamilySearch, 1865–1915. This is the sibling and associate item. Marriage records name the parents, as Ellen's did.
- pli_006: church burials, FamilySearch, 1855–1885. This should find John Doyle and the children who died young.
- pli_007: probate for John Doyle's estate, FamilySearch, 1855–1885. This is an image browse because the collection is browse-only (personCount 0).
- pli_008: probate for Bridget and Martin Kearney, FamilySearch, 1879–1935. The window follows Bridget's lifespan. Also an image browse.
- pli_009: cemetery and headstone records, Find a Grave, 1855–1935.
- pli_010: newspaper obituaries, 1855–1935, for John Doyle, the children and Bridget.

This is a question about the couple's children, not a parentage question about one subject. So the plan has no separate item for the parents' marriage, and there is no hints-review item. It has no fallback links. Items 1 to 4 run first because they are name-searchable and free.

---

This plan looks for the rest of Bridget and John Doyle's children. The 1900 census says Bridget had nine children and only two were still living. We know only one of them, Ellen. The plan starts with the 1870 and 1860 censuses to find the Doyle household and list the children. It then checks church baptism registers, because Pennsylvania kept no civil birth records before 1906. Next is the 1880 census, where surviving children may appear in Bridget's second husband's household. It then looks at children's marriages and church burials, which help trace children who died young. It ends with probate files, cemetery records and newspaper obituaries. Those can name every heir and survivor, and the cemetery and newspaper items run outside FamilySearch.

Next, the FamilySearch searches will run in order, starting with the 1870 census, and then the cemetery and newspaper searches on other sites.

---

| # | Type | Record Set | Notes |

| **pli_002** | Military | Thisted Amt levying rolls (1789–1814), FamilySearch | Name-searchable; list boys under their father's name — **direct parentage evidence** |
| **pli_003** | Military | Volume 004748896, Stagstrup parish roll | Fallback browse if pli_002 is unproductive |
| **pli_004** | Vital record | Stagstrup & neighboring parishes — parents' marriage (1740–1779) | Confirms the couple; doesn't alone prove Mikkel is their child |
| **pli_005** | Census | Stagstrup, 1787 & 1801 censuses | Should place Mikkel in a household headed by a Niels |
| **pli_006** | Church | Stagstrup siblings' baptisms & godparents (1765–1795) | FAN item to identify the right Niels |
| **pli_007** | Probate | Hassing Herred / Thisted Amt — father's probate & burial (1779–1845) | Death date and heirs list |
| **pli_008** | Church | Stagstrup — Mikkel's own marriage & death/burial entries (1779–1850) | Backup route if the baptism can't be found |

---

**Recommended next step:** Execute the baptism register browse (pli_001) and the conscription roll search (pli_002) — route to **search-images** and **search-records** respectively.

## Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark - late 1700s

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

Patronymic Nielsen implies father Niels; the entry must name which Niels. Check variants Mikkel/Michel/Mickel and Blyeberg/Bleeberg/Blyberg.

Denmark_Military_Records wiki and loc_001: levying rolls from 1788/89 list every boy from birth under his father's name, so direct parentage evidence for a son. Denmark, Military Levying Rolls (2513529) is name-searchable; search Mikkel with Stagstrup and born 1779, noting the father's name and parish/roll numbers. Place fields may rank rather than filter, so verify parish.
Fallback if the indexed search underdelivers: browse-only (personCount 0) levying roll volume 004748896 (1789-1814), find the Stagstrup parish roll and the son's entry beneath the father's.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (a Niels and a mother not yet known; identified from items 1-3). It confirms the couple as a unit, supplies the mother's name (her maiden name only if this was her first marriage; check for earlier/later marriages), and its date versus 1779 corroborates the father. It does not alone prove Mikkel is their child. The surviving register volume starts 1763, so earlier marriages may sit in the parish of the bride; also check neighbouring parishes.

Denmark Census 1787-1930 (1401625, name-searchable) includes the 1787 and 1801 censuses, which name every household member with relationship to the head; Mikkel at age 8 (1787) or 22 (1801) should appear with a household headed by a Niels, placing the child with the parents.

FAN item: browse the register (volume 004130616) for siblings' baptisms naming the same parents and for godparent/sponsor names in Mikkel's baptism, who are often kin and point to the father's family and identity of the right Niels.

Denmark, Probate Indexes 1674-1851 (2015318) is name-searchable; skifteprotokoller volume 004392710 (Hassing Herred, 1690-1850) is browse-only (personCount 0); confirm Stagstrup falls in that herred first. Browse Stagstrup register 1763-1814 and later church books; the subject's own burial dates after he was last known alive.

items.guide_markdown:
## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

The question presupposes death certificates. loc_001: statewide certificates begin 1 Jan 1911; collection 1417491 (Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967) is name-searchable. Tree records only birth c. 1814 (Kentucky) and a 1870 Muhlenberg residence, so a certificate exists only if he lived to age 97+. Run one quick name search (Wilkins/Wilkerson/Wilkens variants) to test the premise, not to stretch to a same-name match.

Tree places him in Muhlenberg in 1870 (last known alive). The 1880 census records relationship to head and birthplace; a first census without him (1880, 1900; 1890 largely lost) brackets the death window and shows widow or sons for later probate searches.

loc_001: county death registers in Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 (1804888) are name-searchable but 1860s-1870s coverage is partial; may give date, place, age and parents for a pre-1911 death. Check Muhlenberg and adjoining counties.

loc_001: for a pre-1911 death, probate is primary evidence; Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 (1875188) is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse Muhlenberg will/order books and settlements by volume. Administrator bonds and settlements bracket death within months and localize it. Window runs to 1911 since the death may be late.

Church burial registers, cemetery transcriptions and Find a Grave for Muhlenberg County give death date and burial place and independently bracket the death; a gravestone age near 1814 birth supports identity.
Obituary or notice of a man of about 60-97 in Muhlenberg; may state exact date, place, family. Fallback if registers and probate are silent.

FAN item: identify household members found in the 1870/1880 census (spouse, adult sons, neighbors) and search their own death certificates (1911+) or probate. Death certificates of sons list father's name, birthplace and sometimes his death; heirs named in an estate help confirm this Elijah's identity.

## Lincolnshire, England - 1750-1800

FamilySearch's 'England, Births and Christenings' collection (1473014) is a partial Legacy index: it does not index all records for this place or period, and no records or corrections are being added — a nil there is a statement about the index, not proof that no christening exists; search the parish register itself before concluding absence. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records)

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Mary Dawson, Female, Birth about 1772, Lincolnshire, England, no sources, no relatives. Baptism naming parents is the direct target. loc_001 flags England, Births and Christenings (1473014) as a partial Legacy index, so a nil is not proof of absence. Search Dawson with variants (Dawsone, Dason, Dawsen), Mary, +/-5 years, county-wide since the parish is unknown.

Fallback if item 1 finds no secure match: browse parish registers and bishop's transcripts for candidate Lincolnshire parishes (from items 4-6 once a parish is known), because loc_001 warns the index is incomplete and the register itself must be checked.

Mary's own marriage (banns, register or licence). Her birth parish is unknown and a baptism may not be found, so the marriage entry may give age, parish of residence and her husband's name, and a witness or bondsman who may be kin. Window follows a marriage age of about 18-28.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other: a Dawson couple married before 1772 in the baptism parish confirms them as a unit, may give the mother's surname (only if this was her first marriage; test for earlier marriages), and its date relative to about 1772 corroborates but does not by itself prove Mary is their child.

Mary's own burial entry (and death record). A baptism may not exist or be indexed, and burial entries often state age and parish; also supports the birth estimate. Window runs from last-known-alive to a plausible death age.

FAN item: baptisms of Dawson siblings in the same parish naming the same father and mother, and godparents or witnesses, to place Mary in a family group and identify the parents consistently. Window spans the likely childbearing years of the parents.

Wills or administrations of a candidate father Dawson naming daughter Mary, sized to the father's plausible death from Mary's birth to about 60 years later. Named kin, executors and witnesses are FAN leads. Used to link a child to parents, which the parents' marriage cannot do alone.

If Mary was alive, the 1851 census gives age, birthplace parish and relationship to head, narrowing the baptism parish; 1841 gives age and county-level birth only. Run after items 3 and 5 identify her married name and residence.

**Mode:** Review. Nothing was written. The active plan still has an unfinished item, and the request asked for a recap.

**Question:** q_001 — "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

---

**What is already recorded:**
- The **1860 census** found Patrick Flynn, age 15, in Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill County — consistent with a ~1845 birth.
- The **1908 death certificate** names Thomas Flynn as father; the informant was his son-in-law, James Brown. That makes the father's name secondary evidence (informant wasn't present at the birth).
- The **project tree** lists Thomas Flynn (I2) as father of Patrick (I1), Mary (I3), and James (I4). No mother is recorded.

---

**Plan pl_002 — Status:**

| # | Item | Status |
|---|------|--------|
| pli_004 | 1860 census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch | ✅ Completed |
| pli_005 | Death certificate, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch | ✅ Completed |
| pli_006 | Probate, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch, 1870–1890 | 🔄 In progress |

---

**Next Step: pli_006 — Probate / Will Search**

Thomas Flynn's probate or will could name Patrick as a son, which would constitute direct evidence. The "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" collection is browse-only (no name index), so this requires a **page-by-page image browse** of the Schuylkill County Register of Wills. → Hand off to **search-images** (or search-records) to execute pli_006.

---

**Gaps to plan after pli_006 closes:**
- No item for the **parents' marriage** (which would supply the mother's maiden name).
- No item for **baptism or church records** (Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable).
- No **FAN (Family, Associates, Neighbors) item** — required for a parentage question.
- Thomas's death date is unknown; the 1870–1890 window may be too narrow (could extend to ~1905).

**Other issues:**
- No locality survey exists for Schuylkill County or Pennsylvania.
- q_001 shows as concluded-but-blocked, with an empty proof summary (ps_001).

---

**Bottom line:** The immediate next step is to execute **pli_006** — browse the Schuylkill County probate image volumes to find whether Thomas Flynn left a will naming Patrick as a son. After that closes, the plan should be extended to include parents' marriage, church records, and FAN searches.

**Plan pl_002**

The item is still open because no log entry closes it.

**Gaps to plan after pli_006:**
- The plan has no item for the parents' marriage to each other, which would supply the mother's maiden name.
- It has no item for a baptism or church record. The Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable.
- It has no FAN item, such as a sibling's marriage or a neighbor's record. A FAN item is required for a parentage question.
- Thomas's death date is unknown, so the 1870-1890 window may be too narrow. A parent of a child born in 1845 could have died up to about 1905.

I did not add these items. Adding them needs a supersede or add-new step once pli_006 is closed.

- No locality survey exists for Schuylkill County or Pennsylvania.

**Hand-back:** search-records for pli_006 on FamilySearch.

These are scanned images with no name index, so they have to be paged through by hand. A will naming Patrick as a son would settle the question. After that, the plan should be widened. The next searches would be for the parents' marriage, church baptism records, and relatives or neighbors, and Thomas's death date may need a wider window.

items.guide_markdown:
## Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico - 1880-1920

Although Mexicans use two surnames, most indexed records carry only the first (paternal) surname — search with the paternal surname alone; when the person is not found, search through the parents (a parent search with each parent's first surname, leaving out the child's name). (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org)

entry.rationale: Tree holds only I1 with Birth about 1895, Guadalajara, no parents, no sources. Civil birth registration (loc_001 lists Mexico, Jalisco, Civil Registration, 1857-2000, collection 1918187) would name both parents. Per loc_001 quirk, search paternal surname Hernández alone and also by given names; try variants Hernandez/Hernández, Ramirez/Ramírez and María Guadalupe/Guadalupe/Lupe/Ma. Guadalupe, since the first given name María is often dropped. Window widened for the 'about' birth year.

Catholic baptism entry in a Guadalajara parish (sagrario/parish unknown) states parents and often grandparents and godparents; Mexican naming customs page says the maiden surname is always used, so the entry gives the mother's own surname. Run a parent-keyed search (Hernández and Ramírez as separate surnames, child name left out) per loc_001 quirk, and use browse of parish registers if the collection is not name-searchable.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other, once candidate names surface from items 1-2 (or a search Hernández with Ramírez as spouse surnames). It confirms the couple as a unit, gives the mother's maiden name (check for an earlier marriage of either spouse), and its date relative to about 1895 corroborates, but does not alone prove, that María Guadalupe is their child. Window runs from about 1860 as parents could have married well before the birth.

Subject's own marriage record (civil and church) would name her parents and ages; the birth parish is not documented, so work back from the end of life as well. Search by Hernández Ramírez names across Jalisco civil registration, allowing she may have married elsewhere in Jalisco.

Subject's own death or burial entry (civil death record, Jalisco civil registration, or parish burial) normally states age, birthplace and parents' names; date range runs from the birth to a plausible late death since death year is unknown. Verify the death record's informant, as parent names there are secondary information.

FAN item: births, baptisms and marriages of probable siblings, search by parent-keyed query (Hernández and Ramírez) once parents appear. Siblings' entries name the same parents and godparents or witnesses, who may be kin, and test whether the household is the subject's. Window spans likely sibling births before and after 1895.

Mexican national censuses (1895, 1900, 1910, 1921, 1930) vary in survival and in what is indexed; check which are available for Guadalajara, as a household listing may place the child with parents. No locality collection list gives availability, so confirm at search time and fall back to browse of images.

Full-text co-occurrence search on the surnames Hernández and Ramírez as separate required terms, unscoped across the corpus, executed via search-full-text; Mexican naming customs put the father's surname first, but clerks may reverse them so treat order as unsettled. Aimed at unindexed parish pages (baptism, marriage, burial) where name indexing may fail.

## Hamre prestegjeld, Hordaland, Norway - 1765-1800

Norwegian name spellings were set by the recorder and vary between records (the wiki's example: the given name Sivert written as Syver, Sjur, Siver, Sifuer or Siffuer) — search given-name spelling variants, not just the tree's spelling, before concluding a nil. items.question: Whom did Unna Halsteinsdatter (b. May 1745, Hestdal, Meland, Hordaland, Norway) marry, and when?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. No records have been searched yet.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only her birth (May 1745, Hestdal, Meland) with no source. Confirm her baptism and her father's name (Halstein) first so she can be told apart from namesakes. loc_001 lists Norway Baptisms, 1634-1927 (collection 1467014) but its entry covers Hamre prestegjeld 1765-1800, not Meland itself and not 1745; place_search could not resolve Meland, so check which parish held Hestdal. Search given-name variants (Unna, Una, Unni, Ona) and Halsteinsdatter/Halsteensdatter.

Target record: her marriage. Women then typically married at about 18-30, so window runs from age 18 to well past 40 to allow a late or second marriage. loc_001 lists Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926 (collection 1468080). Search by her name with spelling variants and patronymic forms, also by father's name Halstein; marriages usually in the bride's parish. Verify against the register image.

FAN/indirect: baptisms of children naming mother Unna and a father, with sponsors (often kin). Corroborates the husband and bounds the marriage date if the marriage entry is missed or unindexed. Mother's name may be written with patronymic; search Unna with spelling variants, no surname.

Her own burial entry (and husband's) often gives age, husband's name and farm; useful if the marriage entry is not found or names a different Unna. Baptism is not in doubt here (1745 may predate some registers, so death entry is the check on identity). Dated after last known alive through plausible lifespan.

1801 Norwegian census lists all household members with relationship; at about age 56 she should appear as wife of a named head, placing the marriage as existing by 1801 and naming husband and farm. Cross-check with the husband from items 2-3.

Probate/estate division (skifte) records at the regional state archives in Bergen name widows, heirs and spouses of the farm; parents' (Halstein) estate would list daughter Unna with her husband, and the husband's or her own estate would name spouse. Window set to the lifespans of her father (died after 1745) and of her and her husband.

Local farm history (bygdebok) for Meland/Hestdal typically lists farm families with wives' patronymics and marriage years; a lead to verify against registers, not evidence on its own. Fallback if registers do not locate her.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.
